[h1]Performance:[/h1]

At 1440P, with only Motion blur turned off, everything else on high, the game was always at the 60 FPS cap. Oddly enough, FPS drops (which are few and very far in between) [b]ALWAYS[/b] happen when going to and from certain corridors and certain areas in some missions, where there isn't necessarily anything graphically demanding going on. I was not able to test if it was the same on lower resolutions so it could possibly be a hardware limitation on my end. I've also encountered 3 crashes at the time of writing, which was apparently fixed by not running MSI afterburner + Riva Tuner Statistics Server on the background.


[h1]STORY:[/h1]

- It's the Japanese warring era with demons added to the twist all over again, only this time you play as a gaijin who knew how to swing a sword like a samurai even before landing in Japan, in a quest to take back his beloved pokemon waifu and also erradicate all Yokai messing with the timeline. The protagonist also proceeds to spare the lives of some historical figures that he defeats, only to put them back into circulation. Others even join you in battle, although in their nerfed state. 2 out of 3 of what could be considered main antagonists are rather weak, and the 3rd one doesn't get a proper closure which was a huge dissapointment. 


[h1]GAMEPLAY:[/h1]

+ In the opening level, when both performance testing and getting a feel of the game is critical (while under the pressure of a 2 hour limit that is steam refunds); the masochist in me grinned with much approval when I met my demise twice in a row. The combat system here requires stamina management and patience, is fast paced, challenging, complex and is retardedly satisfying. 

+ The ever distracting Revenant system - where you summon an AI version of a fallen player's avatar for a duel, for that sought after warrior of the west and red demon sets and glory. It also doubles as a warning for danger that lie ahead. 

+ There is an abundance of loot randomly dropped by slain enemies. It also comes from loot boxes, loot crates, war chests and corpses scattered in the game world. Every piece of gear comes with random stats and can be re-rolled via the crafting system. There's plenty of opportunity to upgrade every now and then so your gear never gets stale for long 
until you get that end game gear to end all end game gears.

+ Stat building and several weapon types with unique movesets and skills to choose from, allows you to make a character to suit your playstyle.

+ Mapless almost Labyrinthine level design filled with treasures and deadly encounters that is quite compulsive yet dreadful to fully explore. 

+ Coop Friendly! Those who prefer not to die alone, can summon another player (provided requirements are met) without the hazards of unwanted murderous guests invading your game to ruin your jolly cooperation.

+ Brutal Boss Battles is one of the main highlights of the game, albeit a mix of highs and lows. I thoroughly enjoyed these encounters in the main campaign, but I have no love for the humanoid types on steroids from the DLC. Double boss encounters are also introduced at later parts, and while I'm not a complete stranger to this type of game, Nioh just set a new bar for [strike]cheapness[/strike] difficulty. 

- Balancing issues: Enemy grab moves as always feels cheap. Regular axe wielding enemies often deal more damage than bosses. Mission level requirements skyrockets once you reach the Omi region.

- Matchmaking could use some improvement like showing which mission has an active player who wants to co-op, or an option to allow the guest to narrow down to a region without having to choose a specific mission to participate in.

- Only the main protagonist strips into his diapers when dipping on hotsprings.

[h1]VISUALS:[/h1]

+ Gorgeous character designs, from monsters to NPCs.

+ Environments are immersive and the low quality textures here and there don't really take away from the experience. 

+ Customizable fashion that also transitions to cutscenes.

- 30 FPS capped and almost sluggish cinematics which is a bit painful to watch.

This game is probably the biggest love/hate relationship i've ever had with a game. So many things are done right, so many things are done badly.

Years ago i saw it on store and thought.... is this a japanese version of Witcher? Why does the guy look oddly similar to Geralt? I expected some basic RPG you can zone through and enjoy slowly on the side, exploring the open world map etc. While it is technically correct that this guy is a Witcher in Japan, every other assumption i've had is wrong.

I'd say this is one of the hardest games i've ever played, if not the hardest. I just hit the wall with first DLC mission and i give up here since it quite literally feels impossible, i barely deal any damage and it would probably take me ungodly amount of time to complete rest of the game. It doesnt feel like it was designed for players who want to just finish the game once.

It took me about 80 hours, i finished base game main and almost all side missions (finished only 1/3 double boss fights) and i died over 1600 times. I've used just light armor and spear, kusarigama from time to time as second weapon for certain mobs, no living weapon, no jutsu, no magic, no kodama blessings, no summons nor consumables besides elixirs. I've used ranged weapons for few basic mobs.

This game was in development for over a decade and it really shows. Base game has at least 40 hours of content and is very replayable with 5 different "new game" difficulties which offer way more builds than NG. There is also coop functionality and PvP.

Things done right:

Atmosphere in this game is done really well, it is gritty and ruthless, You will feel like you are in middle of wartorn country, and on top of it you get attacked by demons on all sides, it pretty much feels like being trapped in hell. Cutscenes will provide some respite and remind you that there are actual humans in this world, although you barely interact with them. Otherwise, nothing breaks the immersion or even provides an expected japanese comic relief. It is brutal in both setting and gameplay from start to finish. Story is inspired by japanese history, and mixes in historical events and boss designs nicely.

There is so much equipment offered here. 7 different types of close combat weapons and they all come with various combos and each has 3 stances. Low (fast), mid (balance), and high stance (slow) - which i used most of the time. Combat has some of most depth you'll ever find and is really rewarding once you get the hang of it. Weapons don't feel as limiting and different stances let you adapt to different enemies, so odachi heavy sword still has a chance against faster enemies, and dual swords can deal harder blows when needed.

However, this is just the tip of the iceberg and i wont be able to mention everything because of text limit on review. But there are ranged weapons, ninjutsu and magic skills, living weapon (transformations) and kodamas. They range from simple shuriken, to bombs and major buffs which let you slow down boss movement by more than 50%. And thats still not all.... Like in Diablo, you will collect thousands of items, and they all have crazy stat bonuses. You can get running speed, luck, healing from amarita, aimbot for ranged weapons etc... the list is endless. They arent usual +1 attack stats, and you can build your character like its going on an MMORPG raid.

The game promises being difficult, and it really delivers. Boss fights will feel very difficult, you will die from one or two boss attacks, and bosses come with just right amount of moves to remember. The fights will always feel difficult, but doable. Monster design for most part is fine and it offers some variety, and you need to approach to different mobs in different ways - fast / slow, block / dodge, etc. I also really like how all bosses have only 1 stage.

Game uses small instanced level design and it is very straightforward, you have a small map to clear to reach the boss room, once you kill the boss you go to next mission. You could probably run through cleared map in a minute, but killing all the mobs and boss takes hours. It is an extremely efficent use of maps. Game doesnt bore you with too many collectibles either, there are "kodamas" hidden around the map, and lots of corpses in odd places which you can loot to hear a voiceline how they died. It felt like collecting items was a suggestion and improving the experience, while not necessarily being too annoying. Every map also offers some kind of enviromental hazard, fire, holes, water

Things done wrong:

Im sorry, but controls for this on PC are awful in so many different ways. Firstly, the game shows you only controls for xbox joystick, i had to use a steam guide for menu controls so often. The lock on mechanic uses your mouse movement to switch targets, but also uses mouse clicks for combat, very simple to mess up. The default keybinds for this game are awful and you cant rebind to buttons like mb4/5 either. And most annoying part for me is how stance buttons and ki recovery buttons work, instead of game letting me bind buttons to simply switch the stance and recover ki on seperate ones, it forces you to use very easily misinputed combo of buttons to recover ki, swap stances and attack, which often leads to accidental stance switch.

The combat possibilities and skill ceiling for this game feel endless, you can learn really fast movemets to dodge out of each boss combo, recover stamina and do everything fast, efficently and perfectly. However, for me it never clicked in and i felt like i was barely making any progress because of weird button combinations this game uses as i mentioned above. A lot of bossfights also didn't feel very enjoyable in terms of doing combos, i was finding a small opening in their rotation, hitting one simple combo then running away. Bosses do have poise meter you can deplete and then do your combos, but in bosses where i felt like i had the upper hand, it felt like i was cheating and abusing it (final blow/grapple), so at end i couldn't find a proper balance in most of bossfights. When you think game couldn't get harder, it throws 2 bosses at you at same time, or many miniboss mobs with higher health.

I dont know what to think about this game's way of balancing things. I wanted to have a straightforward difficulty, but it can greatly vary due to many things. As i was reading about boss fights on forums, along the way i read that you can cheese all the way out of this game with LW and Sloth, letting you become invincible and slowing enemy attacks by 50%+, so never used any of it. On the other hand you have to constantly equip higher level gear, which would be normal, if you didn't get very few good options out of loot you get. Actual crazy gear is reserved for NG+, and first playthrough feels like using trial version of gear. 

DLC is locked behind you having to grind for new equipment. I wanted to simply continue from story but gear is very underpowered. No single player game should force you to replay parts of it so you can play the DLC.

Item descriptions are awfully written, and you will need to read extensively on the internet. I dont think its possible to make a decent build on your own or even comphrehend it as a newbie.

Dedicated coop is unplayable for newbies. Die at any point and restart from beginning, each mission is meant to last at least an hour and ends with boss normally.

Side missions feel repetitive and not fun.

Limited amount of heals (elixirs). 

Respawns too far away.

[h1]Nioh is a stellar title playing very much so like Dark Souls with a Japanese theme and a Diablo style loot system; but with some Quality of Life inclusions that make it stand apart.[/h1]

Nioh has you playing as an Irishman named William in service to her majesty Queen Elizabeth on a mission to retrive Amrita - a philosopher's stone type material - and reclaim a guardian spirit stolen from you. Initially you start in England before working your way to the land of the rising sun; a shipwreck claiming your fellow crewmen. When you arrive you find yourself in the middle of a plot to continue an ongoing war between the clans using demonic forces and it's up to you to put 'em down.

Combat feels incredibly similar to Dark Souls, albeit slightly faster and more of an emphasis on blocking over dodges. The weapons on offer are single swords, duel swords, spears, odachi, kurigama, tonfas and axes/hammers for melee; with bows, flintlock rifles and heavy cannons for range. Combat is broken up into quick / strong attacks in three different stances:

[list]
    [*] Low - light attacks with an emphasis on movement and dodge
    [*] Mid - mid range strikes with a focus on blocking and samurai abilities (parrying/riposte/armour break)
    [*] Strong - slow attacks with an emphasis on damage and breaking block / stamina
[/list]

Each weapon handles differently and different foes are dispatched with more ease using specific weapons - mostly due to animation speeds. Supplementing your combat abilities are ninjitsu tactics and onmyo magic. Ninjitsu gives you access to throwing stars and bombs while magic gives you access to powerful buffs, debuffs and offensive magic - magic is a [b]must[/b] in Nioh.

Enemies are plentiful in type using the same array of weapons you yourself use; aside from creatures with demonic attacks. Boss battles require thought and preparation to complete, at times you are often fighting either a boss with minions or more than one boss at a time. Special note that there is a "Grand Tournament" mission where you must defeat a hundred foes - including human, demonic and boss enemies - in a row.

Maps are expansive, albeit not connected in the same manner as Dark Souls. You choose regions which contain missions shared across the same map; so you will be revisiting locations quite frequently. Missions range from monster hunting, item finding and one on one duels. 

Player vs Player (PvP) combat works differently from Dark Souls, as mentioned above, in that there is no random invasions. While you can summon 'revenants' from the graves of defeated foes, they are AI controlled opponents using the gear of the defeated players. Actual PvP and co-op play is accessed through the tea house in it's own menu; and while I have done co-op I have not experienced Nioh's PvP.

All in all, Nioh is a stellar title; pulling off it's mechanics fluidly all while looking and sounding amazing. If you are a fan of the Dark Souls series or looking for an excellent action title, this is the game for you!

- Being a port you might find some trouble getting around the controls or configuring them early. And as time passes you might think once in a while "they could have done 'this' or added 'that' as a quality of life feature" and then realize: the feature actually IS THERE!
Example: You started playing a ranged focused build with unlimited ammo chance gear, so you want to bulk up on ammo. You already turned "replenish ammo and consumables at mission start" in options...

But now you're buying 11 bullets, then exiting the shop, then transfering these to the storehouse to go back to the shop and buy 11 more... and you think to yourself "why can't I buy directly to the storehouse?" YOU CAN! By pressing whatever "RT (right trigger)" is on your setup (mine was ESC after changing some stuff around so I think its probably default 'C' on keyboard) and voila, you can buy stuff, but ammo in particular, in bulks of 999 at a time!!!

You will consistently find the game is full of those convinient stuff that make sense but aren't very noticeable. But they are there and there are tiny notifications telling you how to use them.

You can also find details about stats in weapons and guardian spirits witouth having to consult online, just press the designated button and cycle to the stat you want to know more about.

- Like I said previously this is a port. And a negative side from it is how heavy in memory it is. However, despite what I heard from others, it is remarkably stable for the memory hog it is. Seen it hoover near and even reach 4gigs or ram "nomnoming" in the processes tab and still working. But remember it is a heavy game albeit stable.

- Did I mention the combat is friggin AWESOME?!? You can also "fashion souls" without having to literally wear what it looks like you are wearing by the way. "This loincloth? No, that's an illusion this is actually heavily plated and even has diapers inside for when the monsters frigthen me!"

I wanted to put a minimum of 10 hours in before I wrote a review. Here's my humblest opinion of the game.

I came in LOVING the Dark Souls franchise. Owning all of them across multiple platforms, playing and beating them across them as well. Reading reviews, I've noticed, most of the down votes are only about and hour (if not less) into the game. After playing Dark Souls so much I did have to learn how to play NIOH. A lot of the combat strategy in Nioh does Mimic (for lack of better terms) resemble Dark Souls. THOUGH, might I add, Nioh is not a knock-off.

My review is based on an comparison of Dark Souls which intrigued me to getting this game.
[list]

[*] Combat is deep- You have multiple stances (high, med, low) that change the way you guard and strike.

[*] Controls took a second to get used too- I was used to rb and rt for quick and power strikes but because of the game's mechanics combat is more intuitive using A and Y as your attack controls. This being you need to switch stances in order run heavier longer combos. (I did originally change the controls to mimic Dark Souls, but it was to difficult to change stances.

[*] There are NO invasions or invading- I did like the PVP aspect of Dark Souls. As opposed to leaving "blood spots" you leave a bloodied grave which will appear on other peoples games if your connected online. It will tell you how they died, also the Rarity of loot they were wearing (helm, chest, legs feet, hands, and weapon). You now have a chance to fight the revenant (you as an AI) and assuming you win the Revenant will drop loot depending on they were wearing. I found this fun! btw when you win you get an "Ochoko cup" (basically a disposable orange soapstone) which is a necessity in order to summon friends for co-op.

[*]There are Missions- This was the LARGEST difference from Souls games that Nioh presents. Dark Souls was an adventure that would throw you into a world and let you explore and get to new areas. Nioh has Pre-rendered levels so to speak  that once you complete the mission it sends you back to a map were you select a new mission. You will return to different points in that said map (with different openings and closures) to complete lets say a Sub-Mission. That being said you will have to grind on the same level/Map a few times. (This is my largest if not only gripe the adventure is not really there.)
[*]Tutorials- (I should have started with this) There are Tutorial missions. Be warned though. it does teach you how to use your skill points but make sure you are looking through the whole selection before assigning your points.

[*]Graphics- The Character Models are great! (They better be since you can't make a custom Character) the levels are well made too (again, they better be since a small map is loaded as opposed to an entire castle and outskirts).

[*]More on CO-OP- As I mentioned before you need OCHOKO CUPS. You get these be fighting Remenants. This will allow you to "summon" a visitor from a Shrine (bonfire so to speak) to help you clear the area and fight the boss. I do have a hard time getting summoned into a game that is not on my friends list. It could be because I need to complete more levels or the early levels are to easy or not to many people need or know how to get help from visitors(phantoms).

[*]LOOT- This game has RNG loot. Not often will you find the same stats on a weapon or your armor. There are magic stats that manipulate you gear such as crits, resists, etc... you can also re-roll a stat for money and crafting components at the blacksmith.

[*]Bosses- Are big and gratifying to take down!
[/list]
All things aside this is definately less of an adventure (not saying this in a bad text) than any Dark Souls game is. This game is great fun in its own right. Please comment if you have anymore questions. I know I barely dented what this game has to offer in a review.

As much as I'd like to recommend this title, it's too niche to appeal to most players. Someone once referred to this as "Annoying Dark Souls" as opposed to "Better Dark Souls" and I'd have to say that's even saying it nicely. When I finished Dark Souls 1 a few years back, I felt genuinely accomplished and wanted to try more and more on harder difficulties. Eventually jumping into other similar titles. When I finished Nioh, I just felt numb at the end. Nioh has the foundation of Souslike games and starts pretty solid for the first few hours, but eventually turns into a slog of game mechanics that you have to constantly be aware of if you want to succeed.

The biggest difference between Nioh and other soulslike is that in order to becomes "gud" or successful in this game, you don't focus on your skills as a player as much as learning the inventory system with all of the buffs and benefits all of the randomly dropped loot provides.  You also always stay underpowered as the monsters grow in level with you, which means they continue to one/two shot you even as you gain 10s of new levels.

It all comes down to spending hours upon hours staring at your inventory screen and trying to forge/reforge a perfect item (you'll usually need at least 5 though) and spending more hours reading/watching videos to copy what others have done. Without these perfect builds (based on TONS of obtuse mechanics) it becomes so frustrating to play this game. Not dark souls frustrating where you learn with every fail, more "so I have to go and grind for that perfect drop in some other level so I can reforge it for hours before I can proceed" frustrating. And since forging isn't even fun or interesting it makes Nioh a very obtuse game.

To make things more difficult/worse, wiki for this game is very limited and there have been multiple nerfs over the years to make many builds useless, so all of this becomes a frustrating rather than enjoyable experience.
And without a strong build that can survive a few hits or decimate opponents quick, you end up constantly underleveled and frustrated as even the basic monsters with usually one shot you in higher difficulty levels. 

So even though the game starts as a soulslike and is quite enjoyable at first, once you reach the end of the first playthrough and start to replay some of the missions or do extra content, it just becomes plain tedious as you're forced to start looking up build guides and mix/match stats in your equipment, which in many cases may have already been nerfed. 

I'd probably only recommend this to someone who REALLY likes theorycrafting and min/maxing their character in games and enjoys staring at inventory screen for days, rather than actually playing the game. If you want to just go through the game with random drops and don't want to worry about the numbers, there's only so far you'll get before becoming way too underpowered to proceed.

And to make things even more difficult, after every missions you're showered with 100s of pieces of equipment that's often useless but MAY contain that one bonus you want so going through most equipment becomes a must too...so yeah....ugh...just frustrating, can I just play the game instead?

I really wanted to get Nioh 2 before playing this, but now that I've read it's basically Nioh 1 but with more mechanics to worry about, no. I think I'll just skip

I honestly think this game would be SO MUCH BETTER if they did the following:
-reduce the number of mechanics players have to worry about
-add an actual difficulty setting for people that don't want to worry about min/maxing
-make loot more meaningful or at least make a good inventory system where we don't have to scroll through 100s of items per mission in what seems to be a console era inventory screen
-maybe stop the nerf updates? what's the point? it's not a PVP game
-provide some other way of fun for people wanting to go through the game that don't care for min/maxing

After beating all the Souls games I had a mad itch for more. I beat Lords of the Fallen but Nioh seemed way more promising. And it was, I was hooked hardcore by the combat system and overall fidelity the first 10 hours or so. The combat is fluid, versatile, and deep. The world is interesting, colorful, and a great twist on historical fantasy japan. The graphics and maps look great, all the abilities and enemies sound great and are well animated. Then after playing more and more I start to notice something.....

Its not deep. 

The maps? Since they're 1-shot missions and not open worlds they get re-used for all the side missions. They're incredibly linear and tight. Open areas don't exist because that would give you room to actually dodge attacks. You'll get sick of the same reskinned level being used over and over and over and over and over

The enemies? Re-used constantly. Even the bosses are re-used constantly (in a souls-like? really? bosses are a main draw...) to the point where some are just random enemies in levels.  And after you get to about level 50 you just can run through the maps one-shotting everything you come across, so the game's idea of balance is throw more and more and more fodder enemies at you. Like fighting 6 enemies in a tiny loot room? get used to that times 10000

The loot? Everyone talks about how grindy it is but that's not my problem. My problem is how useless it is. It doesn't matter if you're a light armor or heavy armor user, bosses WILL one-shot you. Spec'd into blocking? Bosses WILL drain all your stamina in one attack. +100 life? +500 yokai damage? You can't tell. There's no feedback on anything and you can play the entire game without learning that your gear is garbage. There are no tutorials, no testing areas to check your damage. Like I said, you can run through levels, upgrading gear as you play the story, 1-combo-ing almost every enemy except the large oni, so its impossible to tell if you're bad until you reach a boss. The lack of information is just appaling. 

You see everything the game has to offer very quickly, and then it becomes a tedious grind. I feel like Team Ninja just didn't have a good grasp on how to scale the game difficulty/late game up compared to other Souls-likes. You can't just add more numbers like in Diablo. 

Honestly, if you're a video game masochist who likes Ninja Gaiden and don't rage quit easily its worth checking out, but don't expect to beat it. Its so long that you just get tired of the monotony and forget to play it every again. As a Souls fan its not what I wanted.

I dismissed Nioh as a mere Dark Souls knock off for far too long.  I am glad I finally played it, as it is a fantastic game. 

Set in late 1500's Japan, Nioh tells the long secret tale of how two westerners factored into Japan's history.  As already referenced, Nioh is strongly influenced by Dark Souls.  The combat, while adding its own wrinkles, is strongly based on From Software's masterpiece, as is the gameplay loop of enemies coming back when you saving, losing your xp when you die, and yes, the difficulty is just as high.  That being said, the combat and the gameplay are fantastic.  

Yes, it is influenced by another game, but it is no mere knock off, it is exceptionally well done.  One large difference between the games is that Nioh does not seek to overwhelm you in all ways, the way the Souls games do.  It has a coherent narrative, a strong tutorial/training dojo, and discreet levels rather than giant maps.  You never have that feeling of being completely lost and wildly out muscled, like in a souls game, for better or worse.      

Nioh does not give the user quite as much agency in its graphical settings as some games do, but it is a great looking and sounding game that runs well.  The game has a ton of meat on the bone, main missions, sub missions, twilight missions, a ton of different weapons to master, each with three different stances, ninjitsu abilities, Onyo magic...  If you find yourself enjoying Nioh you will definitely get your moneys worth.  I got the credits to roll, and did every sub mission available before the last main mission, but did not do any of the post credit stuff.  Not because I was not enjoying the game, I just have way too many games to play and would rather move on to the sequel and other stuff.

After 10 hours, I'd recommend this game wihout any second thought. 90 hours into the game, I'd rather not. Also I'm not sure if I'll be finishing it or not.

PRO
- Gorgeous visuals, especially characters and gear. All the samurai armors and weapons look fantastic, and character models and animations are very well done.
- Nicely designed levels. Linear, but the freedom of movement is enough to not get you the 'running in s tunnel' feeling like in Code Vein.
- Equipment crafting and upgrade system
- A bit unusual, but quite deep combat system. Spamming R1 won't get you anywhere so you'll have to develop some skill in order to progress. Except the KI (stamina) regeneration which is outrageous (see further on).
- Boss designs. All different, all gorgeous. Not boss fights though (see further on).

Neutral
- The plot. It's kinda there, but you really loose nothing if you don't pay any attention to it.
- Music. It's there, it fits the setting, but it's not even close to the level of Nier: Automata.
- Reused levels. You have to go through every area at least 2 times, and sometimes up to 3-4 times. Doesn't annoy me as much as other people though.
- Enemy varieties. A bit more diversity would've been welcome.

CONTRA
- Any stronger enemy can kill you with at most 2 strong attacks, regardless of your gear. And they throw those attacks in series of 2 or 3. This in turn leads to 2 consequences:
  * The life bar is useless. You've been hit - you heal. Otherwise, the second blow is guaranteed to kill you.
  * Getting better armor doesn't do anything. At any point in the game you still die from at most 2 strong hits.
- You can get stunlocked indefinitely. In other words, consequtive attacks can nail you to the spot, unable to dodge. You mash the dodge button in rage while your character is helplessly standing still while being sliced to bits.
- Your attacks don't interrupt attacks of most enemies. A bummer for a veteran DS3 player like myself.
- Because of the previous 2 issues, you can't trade blows. If you try, you get stunlocked while your enemy doesn't. And even if you strike first, you don't interrupt enemy's attack so you still get hit. 2 hits and you are dead.
- Very 'thick' enemies. All the enemies and bosses heve enormous amounts of HP, which effectively devaluates your weapon upgrades. At no point in the game you have a weapon which is powerful enough to oneshot even regular weak enemies, let alone stronger ones.
- Some of the normal, non-boss enemies can (and will) oneshot you. I think this is especially unfair towards the player because of the amount of health the enemies have. You have to hit a large demon like 50 times while he just oneshots you. I'm sorry, but this is a game, not Olympic figure scating where a single error costs you a medal.
- Souls-like system where all your 'souls' are left where you die and you need to go and retrieve them. Imagine getting to your body when all the enemies can kill you with 1-2 hits. And you have to do that time and time again because any little mistake gets you killed.
- Stamina recovery delay. Let's take DS3. When you get out of stamina, you wait a tiny bit, and it starts regenerating. As soon as you have even 1% of the stamina bar, you can already so something, i.e. dodge/roll. Not in this game! When you run out of stamina, you can't do anything until like 40% of the entire stamina bar has regenerated! Now, imagine having to stay still for 3 entire seconds in a fight against an enemy that oneshots you at full health. OMG, SO MUCH RAGE!
- Grind. All but absent in the beginning, the amount of it increases as you progress. Further into the game it becomes increasingly difficult to reach the recommended level for plot missions. So you have to do some missions over and over again multiple times, as even with EXP gain bonuses it takes ages to get enough for a level-up.
- Boss difficulties. Some of the bosses are disproportionally powerful compared to the overall difficulty of the mission. You can reach a boss without breaking a sweat, then die 30 times in a row. And the more you die the  harder it gets because you run out of consumables.
- Consumables don't always get consumed. You try to heal, but it doesn't work because the swing animation didn't finish completely yet, or you are in the last few frames of a roll, or sometimes for no apparent reason at all.
- Detection range of the enemies is quite small. For meelee enemies it's around 15 meters. You can stand there in plain sight aiming the bow for a pefect headshot, and the enemy won't notice. This doesn't apply to shooters which have adequate detection ranges.

I have played the PS4 version and can say it is worth getting the PC version, you get different weapons and its stats are always different. The game has endgame, which is getting the sets of armour you want to get and ethreal rarity, which are the highest rarity in the game. combine it with the weapon you want that offers the best stats and combine them to get the best overall output damage.

Endgame:

The game offers abyss mode, which is a Bloodborne version of chalice dungeon, where you face a boss at the arena. The mode has buffs on the enemy and debuffs for you. Dont let this alarm you as you can enter the plane which consists of removing 4 debuffs or buff from the arena so that they dont have the upper hand. As said above, you can get ranged weapons (bow, cannon) that have their own stats that build your character to be endgame. There are multiple playthroughs that get harder and buffs enemies and debuffs you. Did I say that there are 999 floors in the abyss? You now have no life if you tried.

Story:

Not to spoil much as it can get lost but as you learn more of the lore (via google or in-game stats) you will understand it and sanction you to the whole point of the game. The game will get harder but there are shrines that refill ammo, health etc.

Side-missions:

There are many side missions in the game, some vary from defeating 2 bosses from main game (which is harder, considering the playthrough, but viable), to finding or killing a certain enemy.

CO-OP:

There is coop that allows you to find other players and make them join your game if you're having trouble with a boss or mission. Do remember that you must complete the mission for you to join and help them on the same mission, or they must complete it. You can offer cup at the shrine to summon random player. You can also do twilight missions with random players, this is harder than standard mission but if one of the players die, instead of mission failing, you get a huge blue bar that decreases overtime and requires you to get to your partner and revive him/her. Great feature is when you visit shrines,  they refill the bar at a certain percentage and offer a random buff to you and your ally.

PVP:

The mode is there and gives players starting gear with no advantages, including weapons. There are no stats as it would make it unfair, dodge, counter, parry, strike, you choose how to take out your foe. 

Enemy types:

There are 2 types of enemies. human and yokai, or monsters and each human and monsters are different and variety in each. You may encounter a long range bow based human, with a dual sword based yokai that closes the gap quickly.

Personal statement:

It's worth the money regardless of price. A quick tip of those:

1 - Dodge, counter and parry is everything, even in PVP (you can't counter or parry yokai monsters. In PVE, you can counter and parry human bosses).

2 - 1st playthrough understand the game and try different weapons that you see fit.

3 - Different grace sets are endgame, so you will find them in the abyss, google search comes in handy.

4 - Don't be afraid to use your guardian spirit as it can help. Think of it as going super sayian mode. There are many animals with each unique buffs. You get 2 animals later in the game, combining both with different buff.

5 - Invisibility and silent footstep can allow you to bypass enemies without drawing to much attention, so get it when you can.

6- The game has a discord effect which is hidden, this allows you to apply 2 different elements on a single enemy and it makes them confused and they take more damage from all sources. You can find elemental scrolls around the world or level up your magic and unlock it via the skill tree. The elements are fire, earth, water, wind and lightning. Combine any 2 of these. Also the game has paralysis and poison, which aren't considered elements. 

7 - The 5 elements I've listed has its own traits, applying them constantly to an enemy takes that element damage, for example, applying fire makes the enemy take fire damage over time or applying water makes the enemy take more damage from physical damage.

So, imagine some folks from Team Ninja at some gaming event or other. There's a booth with Dark Souls, and they go check it out. "Wow, you guys really like killing the player!" exclaims one Team Ninja member to the booth attendant. "That's so weird! WE really like killing the player, too!" As this exchange goes on, the player trying Dark Souls dies three or four times more, eliciting bouts of merry laughter from both Dark Souls and Team Ninja sides. Later, we got Nioh.

Yeah, it also has a massive amount of loot drops to sift through, but some handy tools to quickly sort it, sell it, offer it up for experience souls or scrap echoes or whatever we're calling the stuff these days... amrita, you say? Sure, why not.

You play some Irish dude. He's pretty cool. You'll meet an awful lot of famous people from the Sengoku period of Japan's history, and duel most of them. There's also a slew of Japanese monsters to fight and Japanese weapon types to master, as well as a flood of Japanese armor sets to coordinate as you see fit (including appearance swapping... nice.)

Some people say there's no Dark Souls here, but the level layouts feel very Soulsy to me. Explore, find your way up, down and around, sometimes there's a fair bit of sprawl and you check various dead ends for goodies before moving on along the central path... and of course, the bonfire - I mean shrine, next to a door that only opens from the other side... frequently providing a handy shortcut to the next large thing that wants you dead. Repeatedly. There is a good mix of challenge, exploration and streamlining here which I suspect many will take for granted, but which is just about good enough to study. 

Even Dark Souls itself is often guilty of the old "Oops, two and a half minutes' convoluted trek to get back to the boss arena" trope. Maybe it's deliberate, meant to give you time to consider your mistakes and alter your tactical plans, but I always found it flow-breaking and Nioh, by and large, seems to have less of it - assuming you take the time to look around and get those doors unbarred, granted.

It is worth mentioning the difficulty. It's high; you will die, a lot. If that bothers you, this may not be a game for you... or if Japanese stuff is not your deal, this is definitely not a game for you. But if you are a Souls fan and also a Japanese mythology fan, or fan of samurai and ninja weaponry, related martial arts, et cetera... this may very well be a game for you. There is a lot of content for those who take the time to explore... most of it, even, and though some area maps are re-used - some more than others - there are still a lot of them, and the story missions almost always seem to have their own large, unique, sprawling maps.

It can get overly brutal in places, and the struggle to grow strong enough by gear upgrades and level-ups can be tiring, especially toward the end of the latter couple of DLCs' content... but it's all doable, and there is some satisfaction in conquering a mountain of a game like Nioh. A certain amount of zen is recommended to avoid morale loss during repeated deaths. As ever in the Soulsy genre, try to focus on what each death teaches you, rather than growing disheartened.

Also, a controller is recommended. I use a PS4 one on my PC, with the mouse close by for fine-tuning the aim of projectile weapons like the bow and matchlock firearms; this works very well, for the most part.

In summary: A fine game, very content-rich, with vividly animated and skillful combat. High degree of difficulty, could be quite unpleasant to the uninitiated. Recommended overall, but if you have doubts, don't dismiss them too casually; this game asks a lot of the player, more than some can reasonably be expected to put in.

A RPG for action junkies. Take the level structure of a soulslike (Fromsoft games still have better level design), the loot system of a typical Diablo-style ARPG and then incorporate a combat system with as much depth and variety as the best spectacle fighters. The combat is twitchy, fast and demands you time your attacks (Like Ninja Gaiden). Each weapon is useful and fun it's just a matter of mastering them. While definitely challenging (Sometimes cheap with an overabundance of ambushes) its satisfying to play. The story is hard to follow but when your gameplay is this good the story doesn't have to be anything special. The endgame can feel more grindy then you'd like and leveling up endgame gear is an odd process of recycling gear. These don't detract from this being an amazing RPG for us twitchy masochists (Team Ninja fans)

There is a cutscene early on in Nioh wherein Hattori Hanzo pulls a cat out from beneath his robe, takes a moment to look into its eyes, and nonchalantly remarks: “Dawn is breaking”, before putting it back. This is the single best moment in the entire game, and everything that happens afterward is increasingly, maddeningly, tediously awful, like the world's slowest elevator descent into hell.

Hello there, Fellow Imperial Europeans!

Did you ever:
- Wonder why a little fairy-woman-thing stalks your very head?
- Get imprisoned in The Tower of London?
- Talk to a floating cat ninja?
- Get into conflict with a skinny edgelord alchemist?
- Get you rectum penetrated by a turtle-frog-monkey demonic entity's fingers?

If your answer to any of those questions is "yes", you should probably contact a licensed psychiatrist. BUT after that I encourage you to play NIOH.

On a more serious note: 
I was pleasantly surprised by this game. It has one of the most interesting battle system I've ever encounter during my "souls-like adventures". You are not only limited to a certain weapon type and special skills assigned to them. You can also choose one of three stances which are specialised for different situations. Additionally, some enemies are blessed with weak spots (often shiny horns), which can be abused but require you to hit certain spots on their body. This makes combat varied and fun for far longer than I have ever thought.
Nioh also lets you experiment with various, often specialised builds, which add a lot of variety.
That said I have a few "buts". The levels are needlessly complicated and full of terrain hazards. Some of the bosses (mostly the dlc ones) seems to rely on a simple gimmick: they have a metric ton of health and are able to shower you with a barrage of attacks, which can take from 10 seconds to 14 work days. Additionally most of them have some kind of a one-hit K.O technique. That makes those fights needlessly tedious in comparison to other battles.  Lastly, the mechanics I praised before aren't really all that great when it comes to group battles. Pair that with the fact that a lot of late-game missions make you fight against more than one boss or a boss with some heavy hitting mobs and you have a recipe for frustration.

Overall I would say that NIOH is a really good game which is worth playing, but NOT WORTH completing achievement-wise. Smack some dudes, get your share of fun and end it at that.

So, I finally finished Nioh, and man, what a ride.

Let’s start with the good stuff. The combat is honestly, top-tier. This might be my favorite out of all the Soulslikes I’ve played. It’s fast, it’s crisp, and it’s super deep if you want it to be. The game never forces you to dive into every system. You can get by with the basics, but if you do decide to mess with Ki Pulse timing, stances, Flux, ranged weapons, ninjutsu, magic, etc. the game just opens up in the best way. And yeah, it makes you feel like a total badass.

Bosses are tough, but (mostly) fair. If you die, it’s usually because you got greedy or misread a pattern and not because the game cheated. There’s something really satisfying about finally nailing a boss that’s been beating you down for an hour. 

The mission-based structure is kind of “old school,” and I mean that in a good way. Levels feel handcrafted, the kind you can learn and master, and the Japanese folklore/demon vibe is just cool. 

That said... there are some rough edges.

The story is kind of there, I guess? The main character just sort of exists. He reacts to things like someone who missed the plot entirely and is just following a GPS to his next fight. If you only watch the cutscenes, it’s basically: “New guy. New mission. Beat mission. New cutscene. Repeat.” It does make more sense if you read the mission descriptions and logs, but if you're like me and didn’t already know much about Japanese history, some of it might just blur together.

The map design is good and bad. Some levels are genius, but others just test your patience. The stage with holes everywhere wasn’t testing skill, it was testing patience. Also, while we’re on the negatives: every time you finish a level, none of your unlocked shortcuts or shrines carry over. 

Also, it took me way longer to finish because I spent a ridiculous amount of time farming for a full set of purple armor with the “perfect” stats. I was completely hooked on the idea of optimizing my build… until it slowly started draining the fun out of the experience. But that’s on me.

The side content also leans hard on reusing stuff. Same enemies. Same areas. Sometimes the exact same boss - or a double boss fight - just thrown in with four floating firehead dudes for “extra challenge”.

Enemy variety is another weak spot. Most of the game, you’re fighting the same handful of baddies. Occasionally one shows up with a different element or move, but it's mostly remixing what you’ve already seen. And don’t even get me started on the fire wheels. Whoever made those has a special place in hell.

TL;DR: Nioh has some of the best combat I’ve ever experienced in a Soulslike. It stumbles with story delivery, enemy variety, and some frustrating level and mission design choices, and the gear grind can seriously wear you down if you're not careful - although that is totally optional. If you love tough-but-fair battles, Japanese mythology, and deep mechanics with tons of freedom, it’s absolutely worth playing. 8/10

This is a very nice Dark Souls like game, but with itemisation much closer to action RPGs: your weapons have stats, you can craft, you can level the weapons up, sacrifice them and combine them. There are even item sets for you to find or craft later on in the game.

The key concept for this game is mastery: you learn how the levels are laid out, where enemies are, how they fight and how to beat them. Each time you get a little better. Bosses can be pretty tough, but eventually you master those fights as well. Enemies that feel like mini bosses early on will become "standard" enemies that you will fight multiples of later on in the game.

It takes a while for the game to show all gameplay elements, but that's probably a good thing: there is plenty to focus on early on, so being exposed to everything would be overwhelming.

Level design is really good. Enemies sometimes hide around corners, sometimes they have patrol routes, and sometimes things are hidden in plain sight or obscured by your line of sight. Exploration is rewarded with loot, lore and kodama powerups. You'll often find unlockable shortcuts to earlier parts of the level as well, if you look closely enough.

The story is weird and makes little sense so far, but the gameplay is solid and that matters most to me.

Controls for the Xbox 360 controller are good; I haven't tried anything else.
